summary: Specifies the internet Low Bit Rate Codec (iLBC), a narrowband speech codec developed by Global IP Sound. It is designed for robust voice over IP and degrades gracefully when packets are lost or delayed. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: It squeezes a voice into small pieces for sending over the Internet, and if some pieces go missing the speech gets a bit fuzzy rather than cutting out.

questions: how does ilbc handle packet loss
subtitle: A narrowband speech codec built so that lost IP packets make voice fuzzy instead of breaking it.

tldr.problem: Voice over IP loses and delays packets, and many speech codecs let one lost packet damage the sound for a long time afterwards because each frame depends on the previous ones.
tldr.mechanism: iLBC codes every 20 ms or 30 ms block of 8 kHz speech independently, using linear prediction, a scalar-quantized start state and a three-stage adaptive codebook built only from the same block. The decoder conceals lost blocks by repeating pitch-synchronous excitation.
tldr.outcome: The result is 15.20 kbit/s (20 ms frames, 304 bits) or 13.33 kbit/s (30 ms frames, 400 bits) with graceful degradation on loss. The document is Experimental and defines no Internet standard.

today: RFC 3951 was published in December 2004 as an Experimental specification. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the RFC itself says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind. The RTP packaging is defined in RFC 3952.

sections.title: What iLBC Is
sections.content:
RFC 3951 describes the internet Low Bit Rate Codec (iLBC), an algorithm for coding speech sampled at 8 kHz. It was developed by Global IP Sound and uses a block-independent linear-predictive coding (LPC) scheme. It supports two frame lengths: 20 ms at 15.2 kbit/s and 30 ms at 13.33 kbit/s.

The goal is a controlled response to packet loss, similar to what is known from PCM with packet loss concealment, such as ITU-T G.711 at a fixed 64 kbit/s, while keeping a quality-versus-bit-rate tradeoff the RFC calls close to state-of-the-art. The RFC lists telephony, videoconferencing, streaming audio, archival and messaging as suitable uses, and notes that CableLabs adopted iLBC as a mandatory PacketCable audio codec for VoIP over cable.

The RTP packaging is not in this document. It is specified separately in RFC 3952. The two modes work in a very similar way, and where they differ the text writes x/y for the 20 ms and 30 ms values.
sections.plainLanguage: iLBC is a way to turn talking into small numbers for the Internet. It comes in a quicker 20 ms flavor and a slightly smaller 30 ms flavor.

sections.title: Outline of the Codec
sections.content:
The essence of the codec is LPC plus block-based coding of the LPC residual signal. For each block of 160 (20 ms) or 240 (30 ms) samples, the encoder computes a set of LPC filters and filters the speech through them to get the residual. It then picks the part of the residual with the most energy, the start state of 57 or 58 samples, and quantizes it with a plain scalar quantizer.

The rest of the block is coded with dynamic codebooks built from the already coded parts of the residual in the same block. This is what gives coding independence between blocks: a lost packet does not carry damage into later blocks, which is what makes good packet loss concealment possible.

The input to the encoder SHOULD be 16-bit uniform PCM sampled at 8 kHz. Each block is split into 4 (20 ms) or 6 (30 ms) sub-blocks of 40 samples.
sections.plainLanguage: Each little piece of speech is packed using only clues from that same piece. Nothing in one piece depends on another, so a lost piece does not spoil its neighbors.

sections.title: Encoder: LPC and the Start State
sections.content:
For each block the encoder runs one (20 ms) or two (30 ms) LPC analyses of order 10, using the autocorrelation method and the Levinson-Durbin recursion. The coefficients are converted to line spectral frequencies (LSFs), which suit quantization and interpolation better. The LSFs are quantized with a three-way split vector quantizer, with parts of 3, 3 and 4 values using codebooks of size 64, 128 and 128. That costs 6 + 7 + 7 = 20 bits per LSF set, so 40 bits per 30 ms block. A stability check moves apart LSFs that are not ordered, with a 50 Hz safety margin, and the decoder does the same so both sides use identical filters.

The LSFs are interpolated linearly to give a filter for every 40-sample sub-block, and the speech is filtered by these to produce the residual. The encoder then finds the two consecutive sub-blocks with the highest power and keeps the stronger 57 or 58 samples of them as the start state. One bit records whether it is the first or the last such segment.

The start state is passed through an all-pass phase-dispersion filter, scaled using a 6-bit quantizer for its largest magnitude, and then coded sample by sample with a 3-bit scalar quantizer working in the perceptually weighted domain.
sections.plainLanguage: First the encoder finds the loudest stretch of the piece and writes it down carefully, using only a few levels per sample. This stretch becomes the anchor for everything else.

sections.title: Encoder: The Adaptive Codebook
sections.content:
The remaining samples (the leftover 22 or 23 samples next to the start state, then the sub-blocks after it, then the sub-blocks before it) are coded with an adaptive codebook. Its memory holds decoded excitation samples already coded in the same block, running in the same time direction as the target. Sub-blocks that come before the start state in time are time reversed so the same search can be reused. The memory is 147 samples long for 40-sample sub-blocks and 85 for the short one, padded with zeros until enough has been coded.

The codebook has a base section made by sliding a window over the memory, plus an expanded section produced with an 8-tap FIR filter. For 40-sample targets, both sections are augmented with 20 extra vectors that cover delays 20 to 39 by interpolating segments.

The search runs in CB_NSTAGES=3 stages. Each stage picks the vector that maximizes (target*cbvec)^2 / ||cbvec||^2, with the gain magnitude limited to below CB_MAXGAIN=1.3 and, in the first stage, a positive dot product. The gains are quantized with 5, 4 and 3 bits, and the target is updated before the next stage.

Because squared-error matching tends to give a signal with less power than the start state, a final gain correction step re-searches the first-stage gain for better power matching. It may not raise that gain to more than twice the original value, and it changes only amplitude, not shape.
sections.plainLanguage: For the rest of the piece, the encoder looks for bits of sound it has already written down that look similar, then says how loud to play each one. It does this three times, each time fixing what is left over.

sections.title: The Bitstream
sections.content:
A 20 ms frame takes 304 bits (38 bytes, 15.20 kbit/s). A 30 ms frame takes 400 bits (50 bytes, 13.33 kbit/s). The bits are sorted into three classes by how sensitive they are to errors or loss: class 1 is the most sensitive and goes first, then class 2, then class 3 at the end. Class 1 occupies 6/8 bytes and class 2 occupies 8/12 bytes. This ordering allows uneven level protection, which the RTP payload format in RFC 3952 uses.

The frame carries the LSF indices, a block class (start state position), the one-bit position of the 22/23 sample segment, the 6-bit scale factor, the 3-bit start state samples, and the codebook indices and gains for each stage. When a quantization index is spread over several classes, its more significant bits go in the lowest class.

The last bit is an empty frame indicator. The encoder SHOULD set it to zero. If it is 1, the decoder SHOULD treat the data as a lost frame.
sections.plainLanguage: The most important bits go at the front of each packet and the least important at the back, so if the end gets damaged the speech still mostly works.

sections.title: Decoder, Concealment and Enhancement
sections.content:
The decoder reverses the encoder: it looks up and stabilizes the LSFs, rebuilds the start state (undoing the all-pass filter by time reversal), and then decodes the other sub-blocks in the same order the encoder coded them, summing the three scaled codebook vectors for each. A jitter buffer outside the codec decides whether a block was received or lost. For each lost block the decoder runs a packet loss concealment (PLC) step instead.

The PLC described is only an example, and the RFC says other PLC implementations MAY be used because the PLC does not affect interoperability. In the example, a lost block is replaced by a pitch-synchronous repetition of the previous excitation, mixed with random excitation according to how voiced the previous block was, and filtered by the last LP filter. For several lost blocks in a row the excitation is dampened. When a good block follows a lost one, the two excitations are phase-matched and overlap-added to avoid an audible jump.

An enhancer then works on the excitation in 80-sample blocks. It finds six pitch-period-synchronous sequences (three before, three after) for each block, with pitch lags searched from 20 to 120, and forms a smoothed version of the block. The change is limited by the criterion e < b * ||pssq(0)||^2 with b=0.05, so the enhancer can only modify the excitation slightly. Finally the speech is made by synthesis filtering, with an optional high-pass post filter (the reference code uses a 65 Hz cutoff).
sections.plainLanguage: If a piece is missing, the player repeats the last bit of sound in a smooth way and slowly turns it down. When real sound comes back, it fades it in so there is no bump.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the coding algorithm is not subject to any known security consideration. Its RTP payload format, RFC 3952, has several considerations of its own, which are addressed there. Confidentiality of the media streams is achieved by encryption, so external mechanisms such as SRTP (RFC 3711) MAY be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe for squeezing voice is not secret-sensitive by itself. If you want to keep a call private, you scramble it with a separate tool.

sections.title: Reference Implementation
sections.content:
Most of the document, from Appendix A onwards, is a complete C reference implementation of the encoder and decoder, split into files for LPC analysis and coding, codebook construction and search, gain quantization, enhancement, filters and the packet loss concealment. It also holds the constant tables, such as the LSF codebooks, that the main text says must be taken from the reference code.

The RFC says exact compliance with its suggested PLC algorithm is not needed for an implementation to be compatible with the codec specification. It also points to evaluation tools for checking implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The back of the document is the full computer program, so anyone can build a matching one and check theirs against it.

viz.caption: WHAT THE EXAMPLE PLC DOES IN EACH CASE

items.title: Block received, previous received
items.text: Decode normally and save the LP filters and excitation in case the next block is lost.

items.title: Block lost
items.text: Repeat the previous excitation pitch-synchronously, mix in random excitation, and filter with the last LP filter.

items.title: Several blocks lost
items.text: Reuse the same pitch and filters, with the excitation energy decreased each time.

items.title: Block received after a loss
items.text: Find the best phase match and overlap-add the concealed excitation into the new one.
